In addition, the process must be carefully performed in order to ensure no permanent damage is imparted upon the structures. A typical processing methodology will start with short pulses while gradually increasing the power levels while maintaining a threshold breakdown rate (BDR) and vacuum level. Once a target peak power level is achieved at a particular pulse length, the power is dropped back down, pulse length increased and power ramped up, again with the same progress criteria. Due to the advanced nature of modern RF power control systems, this process can be automated and ran with minimal operator intervention. This later point is important from a labor cost perspective as conditioning a high gradient structure can take hundreds of millions of pulses to accomplish and routinely will encompass durations of weeks[80]. For high power RF testing, the linac is assembled into a test stand and connected to the RF drive train, cooling water supply, and mechanical supports. At this point, RF conditioning can begin. Short pulses of low-power RF are coupled to the accelerating structure at low repetition rate. The repetition rate, pulse length and power levels are systematically increased, while maintaining the vacuum below a certain safe threshold, until all parameters reach their maximum values. This process can take several hours to several days depending on the condition of the system. Several examples of world class high power RF testing facilities exist worldwide including the SLAC ASTA test facility, the CERN Xbox facilities, KEK Nextef and in more recent times, the INFN TEX, LANL CERF- NM and RadiaBeam facilities although the later two operate at C-Band. The SLAC ASTA test facility (Figure 37) consists of a XL-4 klystron-based RF source capable of providing up to 60 MW of RF power with variable pulse widths and repletion rate to the structure/component under test. The structure are vacuum isolated from the rest of the system using high power ceramic-based RF windows. The setup ensures that the system is tolerant to high reflected powers and can accept cavities with a wide range of coupling beta without putting an undue stress on the RF power source. Typical interlocks monitoring reflected power, water flow, temperature and vacuum provide protection.
